metadata.title: PLTR Stock Gets Price Target Hikes After ‘Another Top-Line Blowout,’ But Jefferies Sees Better AI Bets In MSFT, ORCL, SNOW Shares

content.text:
PLTR Stock Gets Price Target Hikes After ‘Another Top-Line Blowout,’ But Jefferies Sees Better AI Bets In MSFT, ORCL, SNOW Shares
-
While analysts praised Palantir's continued revenue growth, many expressed caution around the firm's slower rate of bookings.
-
Morgan Stanley praised Palantir's continued revenue growth as "impressive" but said high expectations and slower bookings weighed on the stock.
-
Piper Sandler added that shorter contracts likely explain slower bookings growth and maintained that demand for Palantir's software still "very much outstrip[s] supply."
Palantir Technologies (PLTR) shares fell in morning trading on Tuesday, putting the stock on track to hit its lowest level since September, even as analysts raised their price targets following the company's third-quarter results.
Citi, Morgan Stanley, Piper Sandler and RBC Capital all lifted their targets, but Jefferies kept its target steady at $80 with an 'Underperform' rating, according to TheFly. The firm said that while Palantir delivered a "strong" quarter, the debate has shifted from whether customers want Palantir's software to whether the company can sustain accelerating growth against tougher comparisons.
Jefferies said it sees "more compelling" risk and reward elsewhere in Microsoft (MSFT), Oracle (ORCL), and Snowflake (SNOW). According to the firm, they offer strong long-term growth at more attractive valuations.
PLTR stock dropped around 5% in morning trade and was among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing.
Palantir Revenue Beats Estimates, Company Raises 2026 Outlook
Palantir reported revenue growth accelerating for the 13th consecutive quarter. Revenue grew 96% year over year in the third quarter (Q3) to $2.31 billion, beating market expectations of $2.17 billion, according to Koyfin.
The company also raised its full-year revenue forecast to $8.53 billion from about $8.15 billion, its third increase this year. It expects fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue of about $2.65 billion.
Citi, which raised its target to $265 from $250 and kept a 'Buy' rating, called the results "another top-line blowout," driven by U.S. commercial and government sales. Morgan Stanley analyst Sanjit Singh called revenue growth for a 13th consecutive quarter "impressive."
Slower Bookings Raise Questions About Future Growth
The main concern for Wall Street was bookings, which indicate future business. Total contract value (TCV), which measures the value of deals signed during the quarter, rose 6% year over year to $2.92 billion, down sharply from 49% growth in the second quarter. U.S. commercial TCV increased 11%.
